name: Visceral surface
description: A wide wound through fat, fascia and a thin muscle layer has exposed the serosal surface of a viscus. A serosal arteriole is bleeding and the raw surface oozes. Control them with the least energy and do not injure the wall.

education.goal: Stop the serosal bleeding and the capillary ooze with gauze pressure first and brief low-power coag only where it keeps bleeding, without heating or breaching the visceral wall.

failurePoints.consequence: Full-thickness thermal injury of the wall: a delayed perforation days later.
failurePoints.teaching: The wall is a few millimetres thick and conducts well. Lowest power, briefest touch, pinpoint only, or use pressure instead of energy.

failurePoints.consequence: Wiping drags the clot off the serosa and restarts the ooze.
failurePoints.teaching: Dab and hold. Count to ten before you look.

failurePoints.consequence: Buzzing in the pool cooks a skin of coagulum over the bleeder and cooks the wall under it.
failurePoints.teaching: Clear the field first: suction for the liquid, gauze for the clot, then treat the vessel you can see.

decisionPoints.prompt: The raw serosa is oozing. Gauze pressure, or coag?

options.label: Gauze pressure
options.outcome: Correct: capillary ooze stops with a few seconds of pressure.

options.label: Coag
options.outcome: Heats a thin wall for a problem that would have stopped by itself.

ambiguity.description: How thick the wall is under the serosa cannot be seen.
Serosal vessel positions are seeded per attempt.
